Keeps IREE's chosen pipeline (CPUDoubleTilingExpert / CPUConvTileAndDecomposeExpert / CPUBufferOpsTileAndVectorize) and only overrides the root linalg op's lowering_config<tile_sizes = [...]>. Each round reads the best-so-far RISC-V assembly (LMUL, VLmax, register spills) to ground the next tile-size proposal; pre-compile divisibility gate ensures tiles divide their parent extents (no tail loop); a post-compile check of the IR after iree-codegen-generic-vectorization confirms no tail/masked main path. input.prompt:
I'm investigating why `andesim run --mode hybrid` is ~34x slower in wall-clock than `--mode cycle` for a tiny program (hello world), even though hybrid reports FEWER counted cycles (2734 vs 3573).

Repo: /home/nick/work/andesim. The C++ driver sources are under `src/` (entry `src/main.cpp`, hybrid orchestration likely `src/hybrid.cpp`/`src/cmd_run.cpp`/`src/run_plan.cpp`, process spawning `src/process.cpp`). The cycle-accurate vsim sources are NOT in this repo (they live in an external `hybrid_vsim` checkout); only the shared ABI is under `include/hybrid/`.

Answer these specific questions, with file:line evidence and short quotes:

1. In `--mode hybrid`, what processes does the driver spawn and in what order? Specifically: does it run a QEMU leg (qemu-system-riscv64 + the TCG plugin) to the entry trigger, then a SEPARATE vsim process that resumes and runs the ROI + drains? Or is it one combined process? Show the command lines / argv it builds for each leg.

2. In `--mode cycle`, what single process does it spawn (just vsim running the whole program)? Show the argv.

3. Where does the `window_cycles` / `[pc window_cycles] N (vsim mcycle=... - qemu mcycle=...)` line get printed, and how is it computed? Confirm it is the vsim mcycle delta around the ROI only.

4. Is there ANY existing per-phase timing, profiling, or verbose/debug flag (env var or CLI) in the driver that would print how long the QEMU leg vs the vsim leg took? Look for std::chrono, getenv, --verbose, --debug, ANDESIM_*, HYBRID_* env vars. List every relevant knob.

5. How could I run JUST the QEMU/handoff leg standalone (the developer escape-hatch), to time it separately from the vsim leg? Is there a documented way (a script, a subcommand, or an env var that stops after the drain)?

6. Does the hybrid vsim leg's argv differ from the cycle leg's argv in a way that would make it do extra work (e.g. enabling the Debug Module / JTAG / resume path, loading a state file, mapping a shared region)? Quote the differing flags.

Do NOT modify any files. Report concisely: a numbered answer to each question with file:line citations. If something isn't in this repo (e.g. the DMI restore loop lives in the external vsim repo), say so explicitly rather than guessing.

content.text:
Hybrid is slow because of the QEMU->vsim state-handoff ceremony, not the simulation. It is a roughly fixed cost (~26s here) that has almost nothing to do with your ROI size, and it never shows up in the cycle figure.

Measured just now on your `hello.elf`:

| run | counted cycles | wall-clock |
|---|---|---|
| `--mode cycle` (whole program on vsim) | 3573 | 0.79s |
| `--mode hybrid` (your run, main->_exit) | 2734 | 27.29s |
| QEMU fast-leg alone (reset->main, drain) | - | **0.08s** |

What this proves:
- The QEMU leg is **0.08s**. Negligible.
- vsim cold-runs the **entire** program (3573 cycles, more than your ROI) in **0.79s**. So simulating everything hello does costs under 1 second.
- The hybrid vsim leg therefore spends `27.29 - 0.08 ~= 27.2s`, of which only ~0.6s is the ROI. The other **~26s is the resume + drain handoff**.

Why the handoff is expensive: `--resume-from-qemu` makes vsim write every GPR/FPR/CSR (and V-state if used) into the **halted** hart through the RISC-V Debug Module (abstract commands + program buffer), and `--handoff-out` reads them all back the same way. Each register access clocks the Verilator RTL through the slow debug-module/JTAG handshake. Those cycles run with the hart halted, so they burn real wall-clock but never advance `mcycle`. That is exactly why you see a tiny cycle number (2734) next to a huge wall time.

When hybrid actually wins: hybrid trades "simulate the pre-ROI region on vsim" for "pay the fixed handoff cost." For hello, the pre-ROI region is only ~839 cycles (3573 - 2734), so you save under 1s of vsim time but pay ~26s of handoff. Net loss. Hybrid only pays off when the part you skip in QEMU (boot, big data load, long warm-up) is **millions+ of cycles** - then skipping it on vsim saves far more than the handoff costs. For a tiny program like hello, use `--mode cycle`.

One side note worth a separate look: a near-empty ROI (`--pc-end 0x100076`) still reported **2728** cycles, basically the same as the full ROI. That suggests the `pc-end` may not be taking effect (likely clamped/ignored), so the cycle figure for very short PC windows may not mean what you expect - but that is a correctness question, separate from the speed one you asked about.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -u
SIM=/home/nick/work/vsim_andesim/build/sim_ax45mpv_premium
QEMU=/home/nick/work/qemu_andesim/build/qemu/qemu-system-riscv64
PLUGIN=/home/nick/work/andesim/qemu_plugin/libhybrid_handoff.so
ELF=/home/nick/work/andesim/hello.elf
MMAP=$(mktemp -p /dev/shm hsim-prof.XXXXXX); truncate -s 134221824 "$MMAP"
ST0=/tmp/prof-state0.bin; ST1=/tmp/prof-state1.bin; rm -f "$ST0" "$ST1"
CYC_LOG=/tmp/prof-cycle.log; VS_LOG=/tmp/prof-vsim.log

# timestamp each line with elapsed seconds since command start
ts(){ stdbuf -oL -eL "$@" 2>&1 | perl -MTime::HiRes=time -ne 'BEGIN{$t=time} printf "%08.3f | %s", time-$t, $_'; }
wall(){ awk "BEGIN{printf \"%.3f\", $2-$1}"; }

echo "############ A) CYCLE MODE baseline (no handoff) ############"
S=$(date +%s.%N); ts "$SIM" "$ELF" > "$CYC_LOG"; E=$(date +%s.%N)
cat "$CYC_LOG"
echo "[cycle total wall] $(wall $S $E)s   lines=$(wc -l <"$CYC_LOG")"

echo
echo "############ B1) QEMU FAST-LEG (reset -> enter_pc, drain) ############"
S=$(date +%s.%N)
"$QEMU" -object "memory-backend-file,id=mem,share=on,mem-path=$MMAP,size=134221824" \
  -machine andes_ae350,memory-backend=mem -cpu andes-ax45mpv,vlen=512 \
  -nographic -semihosting-config enable=on,target=native -bios "$ELF" \
  -plugin "$PLUGIN,outfile=$ST0,enter_pc=0x10007c" >/tmp/prof-qemu.out 2>&1
RC=$?; E=$(date +%s.%N)
echo "[qemu leg wall] $(wall $S $E)s  exit=$RC  st0=$([ -f "$ST0" ] && stat -c %s "$ST0" || echo MISSING)bytes"

echo
echo "############ B2) VSIM HYBRID LEG (resume + ROI + drain) ############"
S=$(date +%s.%N)
ts "$SIM" "$ELF" --resume-from-qemu "$ST0" --handoff-out "$ST1" \
   --shared-mem-path "$MMAP" --shared-mem-size 134221824 --shared-mem-base 0x0 \
   --hybrid-exit-pc 0x10047c > "$VS_LOG"; E=$(date +%s.%N)
echo "[vsim hybrid leg wall] $(wall $S $E)s  lines=$(wc -l <"$VS_LOG")  st1=$([ -f "$ST1" ] && stat -c %s "$ST1" || echo MISSING)bytes"
echo
echo "--- first 25 lines ---"; head -25 "$VS_LOG"
echo "--- last 15 lines ---"; tail -15 "$VS_LOG"
echo
echo "--- TOP 20 time gaps between consecutive log lines (gap | elapsed_at | line) ---"
awk -F' \\| ' 'NR>1{printf "%.3f\t%.3f\t%s\n",$1-p,$1,$2} {p=$1}' "$VS_LOG" | sort -rn | head -20
rm -f "$MMAP"

1	// Wire contract between the QEMU TCG plugin and vsim. Both sides write/read
2	// `struct hybrid_state_v1` byte-for-byte through a shared file.
3	//
4	// Stability: never repurpose offsets within a published version. Add new
5	// fields by consuming bytes from `reserved`, or by introducing v2 alongside.
6	//
7	// Endianness: multi-byte fields are little-endian (native on RV64 + x86-64
8	// host). The format is not endian-portable; cross-endian use would need an
9	// explicit byte-swap path.
10	//
11	// C and C++ both compile this header.
12	
13	#ifndef HYBRID_STATE_ABI_H
14	#define HYBRID_STATE_ABI_H
15	
16	#include <stdint.h>
17	#include <stddef.h>
18	
19	#ifdef __cplusplus
20	extern "C" {
21	#endif
22	
23	#define HYBRID_STATE_MAGIC   0x42594841u  // 'AHYB' little-endian
24	// Version 4 (M-ext): append struct hybrid_m_ext_csr after the Andes block --
25	// the writable M-mode CSRs across the whole AndeStar V5 SPA (NMI, CLIC, perf
26	// counters, trap-save, triggers, state-enable, ...), transported forward-looking
27	// and capability-gated per engine. Version 3 (Andes F0) appended
28	// struct hybrid_andes_csr after mmisc_ctl. Version 2 (L11) widened vreg[] to
29	// 128 bytes/register. Readers reject older files loudly (all three consumers
30	// check magic + version + size) instead of mis-parsing them.
31	#define HYBRID_STATE_VERSION 4u
32	
33	#define HYBRID_FLAG_RV64  (1u << 0)
34	#define HYBRID_FLAG_FP    (1u << 1)
35	#define HYBRID_FLAG_V     (1u << 2)
36	// v3: the struct hybrid_andes_csr block carries live values (the producer ran
37	// on an Andes core that implements at least one of those CSRs). Clear means the
38	// block is all-zero and consumers skip restore/re-read/compare of it.
39	#define HYBRID_FLAG_ANDES (1u << 3)
40	// v4: the struct hybrid_m_ext_csr block carries live values (the producer's
41	// gdbstub advertised at least one of those CSRs). Clear means the block is
42	// all-zero and consumers skip restore/re-read/compare of it.
43	#define HYBRID_FLAG_M_EXT (1u << 4)
44	
45	// VLEN upper bound, in bytes: 128 covers the supported engine range
46	// VLEN 128..1024 (L11; also QEMU's RV_VLEN_MAX). This is the wire-format
47	// span per vector register; the LIVE width is the runtime `vlenb` field
48	// below, so one struct layout serves every engine config and the legs
49	// never disagree on offsets. A producer whose vlenb exceeds this ceiling
50	// must refuse to drain (see hybrid_v_drain_policy) rather than truncate.
51	#define HYBRID_VLEN_BYTES_MAX 128
52	
53	// L26: bytes reserved for the V-register transport scratch page -- 32 vector
54	// registers at the wire-format span. The driver maps this many bytes ABOVE
55	// the program's --mem-size (so the scratch sits past the program's RAM), and
56	// vsim's v_scratch_gpa() / kVScratchBytes use the same count. Shared here so
57	// the producer (driver mmap sizing) and consumer (vsim sweep) never disagree.
58	#define HYBRID_V_SCRATCH_BYTES (32 * HYBRID_VLEN_BYTES_MAX)
59

61	// RV64 (8 entries/CSR) and a future RV32 (4 entries/CSR) packing.

63	#define HYBRID_PMP_ADDR_NUM 64

66	// on RV64 only the even-numbered cfg CSRs exist -- 16 entries live in pmacfg0

1	// V-register transport staging: the host<->guest-RAM half of the V data
2	// regfile transfer. The Debug Module abstract-command space has no slots for
3	// v0..v31 (the RISC-V Debug Spec leaves V to the Program Buffer or
4	// implementation-specific extensions), so vsim moves v0..v31 by executing a
5	// vle8.v/vse8.v sweep on the halted hart through the Program Buffer (see
6	// pb_v_data_sweep in program_buffer.hpp, driven by ResumeDriver on resume and
7	// StateDrain at drain). That sweep loads/stores the V scratch region of guest
8	// RAM -- the top page of the mapped span (v_scratch_gpa, L26); this header
9	// provides the matching host-side copy:
10	//
11	//   - stage_v_to_scratch: state.vreg[] -> scratch RAM, called before resume so
12	//     the ResumeDriver vle8.v sweep reads QEMU 1's V values.
13	//   - read_v_from_scratch: scratch RAM -> state.vreg[], called after the
14	//     StateDrain vse8.v sweep so the drained v0..v31 land in state.vreg[]
15	//     (the handoff file).
16	//
17	// The transfer is transparent to the workload: benchmark binaries issue no
18	// transport code, only the enter_vsim / exit_vsim markers. rt_c_v_regs.c is
19	// the reference fixture.
20	//
21	// Pure logic: no SystemC, no DMI bus. Easy to unit-test.
22	
23	#pragma once
24	
25	#include "hybrid/state_abi.h"
26	
27	#include <cstddef>
28	#include <cstdint>
29	#include <cstring>
30	#include <span>
31	#include <stdexcept>

33	namespace hybrid
34	{
35	
36	// Total scratch bytes needed: 32 V regs × HYBRID_VLEN_BYTES_MAX. Sized to the
37	// maximum supported VLEN; the actual per-reg byte count is `vlenb`. Defined in
38	// the shared ABI (HYBRID_V_SCRATCH_BYTES) so the driver's mmap sizing and this
39	// consumer agree on one count (L26/F2).
40	inline constexpr std::size_t kVScratchBytes = HYBRID_V_SCRATCH_BYTES;
41	
42	// L26: the scratch region is the TOP kVScratchBytes of the mapped RAM span,
43	// not a fixed address. Scheme D parks it just above the program's declared
44	// RAM (the driver maps one page more than --mem-size), so no program layout
45	// can collide with it. This is the single source of truth for the GUEST
46	// address the Program-Buffer sweep (ResumeDriver/StateDrain) loads/stores
47	// through; the host stager below copies span-relative and needs no base.
48	inline constexpr auto v_scratch_gpa(uint64_t ram_base, std::size_t ram_size)
49	  -> uint64_t
50	{
51	  return ram_base + static_cast<uint64_t>(ram_size) - kVScratchBytes;
52	}
53	
54	// Sentinel for "no V scratch configured". ResumeDriver/StateDrain default to
55	// it; a non-V handoff never consults the scratch GPA, so that is fine, but if
56	// a V handoff reaches the sweep with the GPA still unset the driver throws
57	// (loud) rather than silently transporting V through a bogus address.
58	inline constexpr uint64_t kVScratchGpaUnset =
59	  static_cast<uint64_t>(-1);

61	namespace detail
62	{
63	
64	// Byte offset of the scratch region inside a RAM span: its top page. Throws
65	// if the span is smaller than one scratch page (a too-small RAM mapping).
66	inline auto scratch_offset(std::size_t ram_size) -> std::size_t
67	{
68	  if (ram_size < kVScratchBytes)
69	    throw std::runtime_error(
70	      "v_regfile_xfer: RAM span smaller than the V scratch page");
71	  return ram_size - kVScratchBytes;

74	}  // namespace detail

content.text:
Confirmed: the sim passes **real per-engine caps** (`andes_caps_from_config()`, starts from `none()`), so unimplemented Andes/M-ext CSRs cost **zero** DMI — that path is already optimal. The waste is elsewhere. Here is the full analysis.

## Where the ~26s goes (measured, per-phase)

| phase | time | work |
|---|---|---|
| startup (reset; no ELF load, mmap pre-filled) | ~0.1s | - |
| **RESUME / inject** | **~13.7s** | ~190 DMI register writes |
| ROI execution (main→exit) | ~0.36s | the actual kernel |
| **DRAIN / readback** | **~11.7s** | ~190 DMI register reads |

vsim reports `214505 cycles simulated` but `mcycle` delta is only ~2734 — so **~211k of those cycles are debug-module clocking** that burns wall-clock but never counts. ROI = 0.36s; everything else (25.4s) is the handoff.

## Root cause

Every register crosses the DMI as **one Debug-Module abstract command + a busy-poll loop**. Each costs ~500-1400 simulated cycles, and Verilator runs the whole core model at only ~8 kHz to do it. ~190 registers x 2 directions = ~380 transactions = ~211k cycles = ~25s.

## Needed vs wasted (for scalar `hello`)

| block | inject ops | needed? |
|---|---|---|
| 32 GPR + PC | 32 | yes (live-in) |
| 32 FPR + fcsr | 33 | **wasted** - hello has no FP |
| V sweep + V CSRs | ~74 | **wasted** - hello has no V |
| M trap CSRs, mcache/mmisc, mcycle | ~11 | yes (correctness/cycle-accuracy) |
| Andes + M-ext (caps-gated) | ~42 | yes; **already optimal** |

`flags=0x1f`: FP and V are transported because the **engine has F/V**, not because hello **uses** them. PMP is correctly skipped (M-mode). The whole **drain output is unused unless `--verify` is on** — the driver only reads back `mcycle`.

## Optimization opportunities (ranked)

1. **Skip the full drain when `--verify` is off** — drain only `mcycle`/`minstret`. Your run does not verify, so the entire **11.7s drain is wasted**. *Saves ~11.5s. Driver passes a "minimal-drain" flag; `StateDrain` honors it. Low effort.*

2. **Transport FP/V by usage, not capability** — set `FLAG_FP`/`FLAG_V` only if the program actually touched F/V before the trigger (`mstatus.FS/VS != Off`, or `vtype` vill-clear). For hello this drops 33 FP + ~74 V ops from inject. Safe at a function-boundary ROI (FP/V regs are caller-saved, not live-in). *Saves ~7.5s of inject. Lives in the QEMU plugin's flag logic. Medium effort.*

3. **Batch GPR/FPR through a memory scratch + one PB sweep** (the way V data already moves) instead of 64 separate abstract commands. *Cuts ~64 transactions to a handful. vsim-side rewrite. Medium effort.*

4. **Cut per-transaction cost** (~1000 cyc each): the abstract-command + poll handshake is the constant. Faster poll or a bulk-DMI path. *vsim/RTL, hard, lower priority.*

## Conclusion

Do **#1 then #2**. Together: **~26s → ~6s** for the common "measure cycles on a scalar program" case, with the cycle figure unchanged. #1 alone already gives ~26s → ~14s.

Note the floor: even fully optimized, the inject of ~50 needed registers (GPR + live CSRs) is irreducible at ~5s, so for tiny programs `cycle` mode (~0.8s) still wins. Hybrid only pays off when the pre-ROI region you skip in QEMU is millions+ of cycles. I stopped at analysis as you asked — say the word and I'll start with #1.

1	// The phase-plan grammar driven by run_plan (F6) -- the C++ analog of
2	// orchestrator/plan.py's Session/Step model, minus the dropped QEMU2 step.
3	//
4	// A Plan is a list of Steps; each Step names an engine (by id, resolved against
5	// the F2 registry), the role to invoke it in (its `invoke` template key, e.g.
6	// "fast-leg" / "accurate-leg"), and a Trigger. run_plan spawns each leg in
7	// order, threads the drained hybrid_state_v1 file forward, and returns each
8	// leg's mcycle/minstret. Under the no-QEMU2-handback design every F6 step
9	// drains, so the hybrid cycle figure is the vsim-leg mcycle minus the qemu-leg
10	// mcycle.
11	#ifndef ANDESIM_PLAN_HPP
12	#define ANDESIM_PLAN_HPP
13	
14	#include <map>
15	#include <string>
16	#include <vector>
17	
18	#include "hybrid/state_abi.h"
19	
20	namespace andes_sim {
21	
22	// The ROI delimiter for a step. `kind` is marker|pc; `params` carries
23	// kind-specific values (e.g. enter_pc, exit_pc) that F9 maps onto trigger
24	// args. F6 only exercises the default marker case (no params).
25	struct Trigger {
26	  std::string kind;
27	  std::map<std::string, std::string> params;
28	};
29	
30	// One leg of a plan: which engine, which invoke role, under which trigger.
31	// `extra_args` are verbatim tokens appended after the filled template and the
32	// trigger args -- the seam for user-forwarded per-leg flags (e.g. the vsim
33	// leg's --kanata), which are orthogonal to the trigger.
34	struct Step {
35	  std::string engine_id;  // "qemu" | "verilator:ax45mpv_premium"
36	  std::string role;       // invoke-template key: "fast-leg" | "accurate-leg"
37	  Trigger trigger;
38	  std::vector<std::string> extra_args{};  // default-init: keeps 3-field Step{} literals warning-free
39	};
40	
41	// A whole hybrid run. Every step loads `elf`; the shared mmap (`mem_size`
42	// bytes, at `mmap_path` or allocated by run_plan when empty) survives across
43	// every leg so memory threads through.
44	struct Plan {
45	  std::string elf;          // path to the ELF every leg launches
46	  long long mem_size = 0;   // shared-mmap size in bytes
47	  std::string mmap_path;    // "" => run_plan allocates one (F5) and owns it
48	  std::vector<Step> steps;
49	};
50	
51	// What one drain step measured (read back from its state file), plus the
52	// leg's captured stdout -- the guest program's own output (UART/semihosting)
53	// rides the engine's stdout and must flow through to the user. `st` is the
54	// full drained record (verify_oracle F4: run --verify diffs the vsim drain
55	// against the oracle leg's in-process, after run_plan removed the files).
56	struct PhaseResult {
57	  unsigned long long mcycle = 0;
58	  unsigned long long minstret = 0;
59	  std::string out;
60	  hybrid_state_v1 st{};
61	};
62	
63	// Aggregate outcome. `error` empty => every step matched its expected exit and
64	// drained a valid state file; `phases` then holds one entry per step in order.
65	struct PlanResult {
66	  std::string error;
67	  std::vector<PhaseResult> phases;
68	  // The concrete per-step argv run_plan built (after placeholder fill, qemu_cfg
69	  // staging, and state threading). Populated whether or not the steps spawn, so
70	  // a --dry-run can print the exact commands without executing them.
71	  std::vector<std::vector<std::string>> argvs;
72	  bool ok() const { return error.empty(); }
73	};
74	
75	}  // namespace andes_sim
76	
77	#endif  // ANDESIM_PLAN_HPP

content.content:
804	### 4.4 Verifying a hybrid run against a QEMU oracle (`--verify`)
805	
806	With the QEMU2 handback removed, the code after your ROI never runs, so a
807	hybrid run normally proves only that a cycle figure came out. `--verify`
808	(default OFF) cross-checks the run's correctness:
809	
810	```sh
811	./andesim run --mode hybrid --trigger marker --engine vsim:ax45mpv_premium --verify your_prog.elf
812	# ...
813	# [marker window_cycles] 46  (vsim mcycle=... - qemu mcycle=...)
814	# [state-diff] PASS: 109 fields match (counters and passthrough CSRs excluded)
815	# [verify] PASS: vsim drain matches the QEMU oracle
816	```
817	
818	How it works: after the normal run, the same ELF re-runs on pure QEMU (the
819	oracle) with the plugin draining at the ROI exit boundary, sampled at the
820	exact pc where vsim halted. The pre-ROI path is QEMU in both runs, so the
821	ROI inputs are identical -- any architectural divergence inside the ROI
822	(RTL bug, state-restore bug, drain bug) shows up as a field mismatch and
823	the run exits non-zero, listing each differing field:
824	
825	```
826	[state-diff] x10: ref=0x3d got=0x0
827	[state-diff] FAIL: 1 mismatch(es) (115 fields compared)
828	```
829

### 4.4 Verifying a hybrid run against a QEMU oracle (`--verify`)

With the QEMU2 handback removed, the code after your ROI never runs, so a
hybrid run normally proves only that a cycle figure came out. `--verify`
(default OFF) cross-checks the run's correctness:

```sh
./andesim run --mode hybrid --trigger marker --engine vsim:ax45mpv_premium --verify your_prog.elf
# ...
# [marker window_cycles] 46  (vsim mcycle=... - qemu mcycle=...)
# [state-diff] PASS: 109 fields match (counters and passthrough CSRs excluded)
# [verify] PASS: vsim drain matches the QEMU oracle
```

How it works: after the normal run, the same ELF re-runs on pure QEMU (the
oracle) with the plugin draining at the ROI exit boundary, sampled at the
exact pc where vsim halted. The pre-ROI path is QEMU in both runs, so the
ROI inputs are identical -- any architectural divergence inside the ROI
(RTL bug, state-restore bug, drain bug) shows up as a field mismatch and
the run exits non-zero, listing each differing field:

```
[state-diff] x10: ref=0x3d got=0x0
[state-diff] FAIL: 1 mismatch(es) (115 fields compared)
```

What is compared: pc, all GPRs, all FPRs (when FP state is live), the V
CSRs and full vector registers (when V state is live), and the writable
M-mode CSRs that round-trip through the handoff -- `mscratch` (L23) and
`mepc`/`mcause`/`mtval`/`mie` (L24), restored at resume and re-read at
drain. What is not:

- `mcycle`/`minstret` -- the engines count differently by design;
- `mip` -- restored and re-read, but its pending bits are hardware-driven
  (the timer bit tracks elapsed time, which differs between QEMU's
  functional clock and vsim's cycle clock), so a compare would
  false-positive;
- `mstatus`, `mtvec` -- passthrough: vsim restores the QEMU1 entry snapshot value; both sides hold the same bits by construction so comparing is trivially true but not useful;
- `satp`, `medeleg`/`mideleg` -- S-mode CSRs, not implemented on the default M-only engine. The privilege level itself IS compared: both
  sides drain the real one (L6), so a wrong-privilege resume shows up as

content.text:
`/simplify → 4 cleanup agents in parallel → apply the fixes`

You are improving the quality of the changed code, not hunting for bugs. Review
it for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude issues, then fix what you
find. Do not look for correctness bugs — that is what `/code-review` is for.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Review (4 cleanup agents in parallel)

Launch **4 independent review agents** via the Agent tool, all in a
single message so they run concurrently. Pass each agent the diff and one of
the four angles below. Each returns its findings with `file`, `line`, a
one-line `summary`, and the concrete cost (what is duplicated, wasted, or
harder to maintain).

### Reuse

Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change is implemented at the right depth, not as a fragile
bandaid. Special cases layered on shared infrastructure are a sign the fix
isn't deep enough — prefer generalizing the underlying mechanism over adding
special cases.

## Phase 2 — Apply the fixes

Wait for all four agents to complete, dedup findings that point at the same
line or mechanism, and fix each remaining one directly. Skip any finding whose
fix would change intended behavior, require changes well outside the reviewed
diff, or that you judge to be a false positive — note the skip rather than
arguing with it. Finish with a brief summary of what was fixed and what was
skipped (or confirm the code was already clean).

## REUSE review findings

Scope reviewed: the `drain-minimal` fast path across both repos. I read `state_drain.hpp` fully, `resume_driver.hpp` (halt helpers), `driver/test_check.hpp`, and surveyed the driver's argv-test assertion norms. Three reuse findings, ordered by cost.

---

### Finding 1 — Duplicated halt-and-wait sequence (real duplication, MEDIUM)

`/home/nick/work/vsim_andesim/src/hybrid/state_drain.hpp:172-175`

Summary: `drain_counters_only` opens with the exact 3-line halt sequence already in `drain()` at lines 45-48 — byte-for-byte identical except the poll's debug string (`"StateDrain halt"` vs `"StateDrain halt (minimal)"`):

```cpp
bus_.write(RD::kDmcontrol, RD::kDmcontrolDmactive);
bus_.write(RD::kDmcontrol, RD::kDmcontrolDmactive | RD::kDmcontrolHaltreq);
poll_until_set(bus_, RD::kDmstatus, RD::kDmstatusAllhalted, "...");
```

Cost: the DM halt protocol (dmactive must transition 0->1 in its own write before haltreq is honored, per the Debug Spec — see the comment at `resume_driver.hpp:113-115`) is now written in three places: `drain()`, `drain_counters_only()`, and `ResumeDriver::resume()` (`resume_driver.hpp:115-117`). If the halt handshake ever changes (e.g. an added `hartsel`/`ndmreset` step or a dmstatus retry), all three must change in lockstep; the new copy makes the third silent drift point.

Use instead: extract a private `StateDrain` helper, e.g. `void halt(const char* ctx)`, holding the three lines, and call it from both `drain()` and `drain_counters_only()`. This is the same pattern `ResumeDriver` already established with its private `request_halt()` (`resume_driver.hpp:302-305`) — note `request_halt()` is only the single `dmactive|haltreq` write and is `private`, so `StateDrain` cannot reuse it directly; the correct move is a sibling `StateDrain::halt()` that mirrors that pattern at the full-sequence granularity.

---

### Finding 2 — Duplicated counter-read pair (minor / borderline, LOW)

`/home/nick/work/vsim_andesim/src/hybrid/state_drain.hpp:178-181`

Summary: the two counter reads in `drain_counters_only`

```cpp
state.mcycle   = read_register_64(bus_, regno_csr(RD::kCsrMcycle),   "StateDrain mcycle");
state.minstret = read_register_64(bus_, regno_csr(RD::kCsrMinstret), "StateDrain minstret");
```

are the same two reads `drain_with_passthrough` already does at lines 113-114 (only difference: the new copy passes an extra debug-string argument that the originals omit).

Cost: low. It is two lines against a stable, single-source CSR pair; a leak (e.g. needing `mcycleh`/`minstreth` high-half handling on RV32, or reading them under a different command sequence) would have to be fixed twice. Not worth its own helper on its own.

Recommendation: this falls out for free if Finding 1 is taken further — the natural shared unit is a private `read_counters_into(hybrid_state_v1& s)` covering the two reads, called by both `drain_with_passthrough` and `drain_counters_only`. If only one extraction is done, prefer the halt helper (Finding 1); folding the counters in is a cheap add-on but not mandatory.

---

### Finding 3 — Local `has` linear-search lambda reinvents `std::ranges::find` (real, LOW-MEDIUM)

`/home/nick/work/andesim/driver/hybrid_test.cpp:181-184`

Summary: the test defines a hand-rolled membership lambda:

```cpp
auto has = [](const std::vector<std::string>& v, const char* s) {
  for (const auto& x : v) if (x == s) return true;
  return false;
};
```

Cost: a new local linear-search reimplementation of vector containment. I confirmed there is no `contains`/`has` helper in `driver/test_check.hpp` (the shared test harness) nor anywhere adjacent, so this is genuinely net-new. It also sits in the same test file whose other block (the diff just above, lines 150-167) asserts the same `--drain-minimal` presence with the existing `check_eq` exact-vector helper — so the file now mixes two membership idioms for the same flag.

Existing approach to use instead: `std::ranges::find(v, s) != v.end()` (or `std::ranges::any_of`) inline, dropping the lambda. Caveat for accuracy: `std::ranges::find` is NOT yet a codebase norm in the driver — the only `std::find` use is `hotloops.cpp:590`, and these tests deliberately avoid `<algorithm>` (`hybrid_test.cpp` includes only `<string>`/`<vector>`; using ranges::find would add an `#include <algorithm>`). So the cleaner reuse is one of:
- (preferred, zero new include, matches the block right above it) assert presence via the existing `check_eq` exact-expected-vector style already used at lines 150-167; or
- if a generic predicate is wanted across argv tests, add a small `contains(const std::vector<std::string>&, std::string_view)` to `test_check.hpp` next to `check_eq` so every argv-shaped test (`run_test`, `plan_test`, `hybrid_test`) shares one helper instead of each growing its own lambda.

I'd flag the inline `std::ranges::find` suggestion as the weakest of the three, precisely because it isn't the established norm here; the `check_eq` route is the in-codebase reuse.

---

Net: 2 of the 3 angles you named are real duplication worth fixing (the halt sequence is the strongest; the `has` lambda is genuine but low-cost). The counter-read pair (#2) is borderline and best handled only as a rider on the #1 extraction. Nothing in the change is so duplicative as to block; the halt helper is the one I'd ask for before merge.</result>

skills.name: simplify
skills.content:
`/simplify → 4 cleanup agents in parallel → apply the fixes`

You are improving the quality of the changed code, not hunting for bugs. Review
it for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude issues, then fix what you
find. Do not look for correctness bugs — that is what `/code-review` is for.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Review (4 cleanup agents in parallel)

Launch **4 independent review agents** via the Agent tool, all in a
single message so they run concurrently. Pass each agent the diff and one of
the four angles below. Each returns its findings with `file`, `line`, a
one-line `summary`, and the concrete cost (what is duplicated, wasted, or
harder to maintain).

### Reuse

Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change is implemented at the right depth, not as a fragile
bandaid. Special cases layered on shared infrastructure are a sign the fix
isn't deep enough — prefer generalizing the underlying mechanism over adding
special cases.

## Phase 2 — Apply the fixes

Wait for all four agents to complete, dedup findings that point at the same
line or mechanism, and fix each remaining one directly. Skip any finding whose
fix would change intended behavior, require changes well outside the reviewed
diff, or that you judge to be a false positive — note the skip rather than
arguing with it. Finish with a brief summary of what was fixed and what was
skipped (or confirm the code was already clean).

- **FP** (lines 295-301): `has_fp` is true if any `v->fpr[i]` handle resolved — i.e. QEMU advertised the FPU. Set whenever the engine *has* F, regardless of whether the program touched it.
- **V** (lines 361-403): `hybrid_v_drain_policy` decides from handle truthiness (`vlenb` exists + V CSR/reg handles exist) — again capability, not usage.

Before I propose the exact gate, I need to confirm the *usage signal* actually distinguishes scalar hello. Let me verify hello's real `mstatus.FS/VS` and `vtype` at the boundary instead of guessing.

/* B7: pure decision function for the QEMU plugin V-state drain gate.
 *
 * The plugin uses one `qemu_plugin_register*` handle per architectural V
 * register. Each handle is non-NULL iff the gdbstub feature XML
 * advertised that register at plugin init. The original gate at
 * hybrid_handoff.c:296 tested `if (v->vlenb && s.vlenb > 0)` which
 * silently omits the V block when:
 *   - vlenb was not advertised but vtype/vl were (partial V), or
 *   - vlenb was advertised but read as zero (V disabled at runtime).
 *
 * Mixing the "stub broke" case with the "V disabled" case loses
 * information; the partial-advertisement case should refuse rather than
 * pretend V is absent (the resume side then mis-restores).
 *
 * This header is pure C, no QEMU plugin dependency, so it can be unit-
 * tested from a host C++ doctest.
 */
#ifndef HYBRID_V_DRAIN_POLICY_H
#define HYBRID_V_DRAIN_POLICY_H

#include <stdint.h>

#include "hybrid/state_abi.h"  /* HYBRID_VLEN_BYTES_MAX: the L11 ceiling */

#ifdef __cplusplus
extern "C" {
#endif

typedef enum {
    HYBRID_V_DRAIN_OK = 0,      /* proceed: copy full V block into state */
    HYBRID_V_DRAIN_SKIP = 1,    /* no V at all; do not set HYBRID_FLAG_V */
    HYBRID_V_DRAIN_ABORT = 2,   /* partial advertisement; refuse to drain */
} HybridVDrainPolicy;

/* Decide whether to drain the V block.
 *
 * has_vlenb:    1 iff the stub advertised the vlenb register handle.
 * has_other_v:  1 iff ANY of vtype/vl/vstart/vxsat/vxrm/vcsr/vreg[*] was
 *               advertised (i.e. some V state is visible).
 * vlenb_value:  the value read from vlenb (only meaningful when has_vlenb).
 */
static inline HybridVDrainPolicy
hybrid_v_drain_policy(int has_vlenb, int has_other_v, uint64_t vlenb_value)
{
    /* Truth table (see v_drain_policy.test.cpp):
     *   has_vlenb=0, has_other_v=0            -> SKIP   (no V)
     *   has_vlenb=0, has_other_v=1            -> ABORT  (partial advertisement)
     *   has_vlenb=1, has_other_v=0            -> SKIP   (nothing to drain)
     *   has_vlenb=1, has_other_v=1, vlenb=0   -> SKIP   (V disabled at runtime)
     *   has_vlenb=1, has_other_v=1, vlenb>MAX -> ABORT  (L11: wire format
     *                                            cannot hold this VLEN; never
     *                                            truncate silently)
     *   has_vlenb=1, has_other_v=1, otherwise -> OK
     */
    if (!has_vlenb && has_other_v) return HYBRID_V_DRAIN_ABORT;
    if (!has_other_v)              return HYBRID_V_DRAIN_SKIP;
    if (vlenb_value == 0)          return HYBRID_V_DRAIN_SKIP;
    if (vlenb_value > HYBRID_VLEN_BYTES_MAX) return HYBRID_V_DRAIN_ABORT;
    return HYBRID_V_DRAIN_OK;
}

#ifdef __cplusplus
}
#endif

#endif  /* HYBRID_V_DRAIN_POLICY_H */

content.text:
Confirmed the layout. crt0 eagerly sets **both** `mstatus.FS=Initial` and `mstatus.VS=Initial` at boot (crt0.S:76-82). This is the crux: a naive "FS/VS != Off" usage gate would **still transport** for scalar hello, because FS/VS are never Off — they sit at Initial.

The linchpin question is whether QEMU's FS/VS *dirty-tracking* is trustworthy (Initial stays Initial when unused, promotes to Dirty/Clean on real use). I must verify that empirically, not assume it. Let me drain a scalar fixture and an FP fixture and compare.

content.text:
## #2: gate FP/V transport on usage, not capability

**Two signals, both already in the drained state (no extra QEMU reads):**
- **FP**: transport only if `mstatus.FS >= Clean (2)`. Skip when `Off` or `Initial`.
- **V**: transport only if `vtype.vill == 0` (a `vsetvl` configured V). Skip when `vill` set.

**Why not the obvious `FS/VS != Off`:** crt0 eagerly enables both (`crt0.S:76-82` sets `FS=Initial`, `VS=Initial`), so neither is ever `Off`. A `!= Off` gate would never skip anything. I drained 4 fixtures to find what *does* distinguish usage:

| fixture | uses | FS | VS | vtype.vill | FP gate | V gate |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `rt_c_hello` | nothing | 1 Initial | **2 Clean** | 1 | skip | skip |
| `rt_c_matmul` | int only | 1 Initial | **2 Clean** | 1 | skip | skip |
| `rt_c_fcsr` | FP | **3 Dirty** | 2 Clean | 1 | **send** | skip |
| `rt_c_v_regs` | V | 1 Initial | **3 Dirty** | **0** | skip | **send** |

Two findings drive the design:
- `mstatus.VS` is **useless** for V: it reads `Clean(2)` even on scalar hello/matmul. So I use `vtype.vill` instead -- the architectural "V was configured" bit, which is clean (1 on every non-V program, 0 only on the V user).
- `mstatus.FS` **is** reliable for FP: `Initial` on every non-FP program, `Dirty` only on the FP user.

**Correctness (safe for the documented trap-free, function-boundary ROI):**
- `FS ∈ {Off, Initial}` means FP regs hold no live program state (Initial = enabled-but-untouched, regs at reset). The ROI cannot read live-in FP -- caller-saved, and any read-before-write sees reset zeros on both engines.
- `vill == 1` means every vector op faults until a `vsetvl` runs, so there is no live-in V data the ROI can read. A ROI that uses V issues its own `vsetvl` first.

**Payoff for hello:** flags `0x1f -> 0x19` (FP+V cleared). Inject drops 33 FP abstract-cmd writes + the V block (`vsetvl` + 32-reg `vle8` Program-Buffer sweep); drain drops the matching `vse8` sweep. This is the ~7.5s inject saving. `fcsr` still sends FP, `v_regs` still sends V -- no regression.

**Where:** `qemu_plugin/hybrid_handoff.c` `drain_state_into`, lines 301 (FP flag) and 395 (V flag/copy). Cleanest: add two pure predicates `hybrid_fp_live(mstatus)` / `hybrid_v_live(vtype)` next to `hybrid_v_drain_policy` (same testable-header pattern), unit-test them, then gate the two flags. **Always-on, no CLI flag** -- unlike #1 it loses nothing any consumer reads, and it is correct in `--verify` too (skipped blocks aren't compared).

Want me to implement it (TDD: predicates + failing tests first)?

content.text:
Yes -- in the `.riscv.attributes` section (`Tag_RISCV_arch`, the full ISA string) plus the `e_flags` float-ABI bits. But it records what the program was **compiled with**, not what it **used**, and for this toolchain that only helps V, not FP:

| fixture | uses | arch has `f`/`d` | arch has `v` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `rt_c_hello` | nothing | **yes** `f2p2_d2p2` | no |
| `rt_c_matmul` | int only | **yes** `f2p2_d2p2` | no |
| `rt_c_fcsr` | FP | yes | no |
| `rt_c_v_regs` | V | yes | **yes** `v1p0` |

**The catch for FP:** the Andes toolchain builds everything `lp64d` (`e_flags = double-float ABI`), so `f2p2_d2p2` is in the arch string of **every** fixture -- including scalar hello and integer matmul that never touch an FP register. So reading the ELF tells you "FP present" for hello and you would still transport all 33 FP regs. The ELF **cannot** save the FP cost. Only the runtime `mstatus.FS=Initial` signal distinguishes hello (unused) from fcsr (`FS=Dirty`).

**For V it works here, but over-approximates:** only `rt_c_v_regs` carries `v1p0`, because the build adds `v` to `-march` only for V fixtures. So "no `v` in arch" correctly skips hello/matmul/fcsr. But it is weaker than `vtype.vill`: a program compiled `-march=rv64gcv` that does **not** use V in the ROI still has `v1p0` in the ELF -> ELF says transport, `vtype.vill=1` says skip. The runtime bit is strictly more precise, and it is already in the drained state (no ELF parsing, no plumbing arch into the plugin).

**Bottom line:**
- **FP** -- the ELF is no help under the default `gc`/lp64d build; you need `mstatus.FS >= Clean`.
- **V** -- `vtype.vill == 0` dominates the ELF check (more precise, zero extra cost).

The ELF arch string is only useful as a redundant *conservative pre-filter* (no `f` in arch ⟹ definitely no FP, skip for sure) -- but that never fires for our fixtures because they are all built `f_d`. It would only pay off for users who compile bare-metal `-march=rv64imac` (no FP at all), and in that case the runtime `FS` signal skips it anyway.

So: keep the runtime-signal plan. The ELF doesn't add precision the CSRs don't already give for free.

136	{

138	    bus.write(kDmiData1, static_cast<uint32_t>((value >> 32) & 0xffffffffu));

content.text:
Read all four transfer files plus the SystemC bus. The framing "DMI vs Program Buffer" is the wrong axis -- here's why.

## The PB is not an alternative to DMI -- it runs *over* DMI

Both mechanisms bottom out in the same `SystemCDmiBus`: every `bus.write`/`bus.read` is one AHB transaction to the Debug Module, and `drain()` spins `sc_start` (simulates the whole SoC) until that transaction finishes. So:

- **Abstract command** (one GPR/FPR/CSR): `data0` write + `data1` write + `command` write + **busy-poll** (`poll_until_clear` reads `abstractcs` in a loop, each read advancing sim time until the DM finishes).
- **PB execution** (one sweep step): N `progbuf` writes + `command` write + the **same busy-poll**.

Same shape, same poll. The poll is the cost: it spins the Verilated DM for however many cycles the op takes (~500-1400 sim cycles each, measured earlier). Wall-clock per op = that cycle count x wall-clock-per-simulated-cycle.

**So performance is governed by one number: the count of halt-mode command round-trips, not the bytes moved.** ~190 round-trips per direction x ~1000 cycles each = ~99% of the inject/drain wall-clock. Moving 8 bytes (one abstract CSR) and running one PB instruction cost about the same.

## The one truly free channel: the shared mmap

The driver writes guest RAM directly through the `/dev/shm` mmap -- zero DMI. V **data** already exploits this (`stage_v_to_scratch` memcpy's all 32 vregs into the scratch page). But the **sweep** that pulls scratch into the regfile still costs **one PB exec per register**, because `vle8.v`/`vse8.v` hard-code the target `vd`. So V is the worst offender per byte: ~66 round-trips for the data that rode the mmap for free.

## Cost by storage strategy

| what | mechanism today | round-trips | byte channel |
|---|---|---|---|
| GPR/FPR/CSR | abstract command, one per reg | 1 each (~115 total) | through DMI `data0/1` |
| V scalar CSRs | abstract + PB (vsetvl) | ~7 | DMI |
| V data v0..v31 | mmap stage + PB `vle8`/`vse8` sweep | **1 PB exec per reg (~66)** | mmap (free) |

## Levers that actually cut round-trips (if you pursue HOW later)

1. **V LMUL grouping** -- `vsetvl e8,m8` then one `vle8.v v0` loads v0..v7 in a single instruction. 32 regs -> **4 PB execs** instead of 32. Standard RVV, biggest structural win. Caveat: scratch must be packed at `vlenb` stride, not the 128-byte wire stride.
2. **Block-load GPR/FPR** -- stage 32 values in a scratch block (mmap, free), then 2-3 PB runs of `ld`/`fld` (15 slots each) instead of 63 abstract commands. Caveat: the base/scratch GPRs must be restored last.
3. **autoexec + aarpostincrement** -- stream a contiguous reg range with one command setup and no per-reg poll (DM auto-advances `regno`, auto-re-executes on each `data0` write). Caveat: optional DM features -- must verify the vsim DM implements `abstractauto`/`aarpostincrement` before relying on it.
4. **(floor) Verilator regfile backdoor** -- force the RTL nets directly, bypassing the DM entirely. Fastest possible, but throws away the real-debug-path fidelity the design deliberately chose; RTL-version-fragile. Mention only as the theoretical limit.

## Priority

Gating (#2) deletes whole blocks -- FP ~34 round-trips, V ~66 -- for ~zero code risk, so it is the biggest bang per effort. The round-trip *restructuring* above (LMUL-group V, block-load GPR/FPR) is the next tier and is where "how you store" pays off, but it is harder and touches the resume/drain RTL path. Do #2 first; reach for LMUL grouping if V-heavy workloads still dominate after that.

我用簡單比喻。

**一句話:** DMI 和 Program Buffer 不是兩條路,一快一慢。它們是**同一條慢路**。慢的原因是「來回幾次」,不是用哪個方法。

## 比喻:慢郵局

把資料放進 vsim 的 CPU,像用**一間很慢的郵局寄包裹**:

- 寄 1 個包裹 (= 搬 1 個 register),要排隊等 ~1000 拍。
- 包裹大小不重要。**排隊等待**才是花時間的地方。

我們每個方向寄 ~190 個包裹。190 × ~1000 拍 = 幾乎全部的慢時間。

所以速度只看一件事:**寄幾個包裹**。不是看包裹種類,不是看大小。

## 想快 = 寄更少包裹

兩個方法:

1. **#2 (我們在討論的)** -- 不要寄沒人要的包裹。現在不管程式有沒有用 FP/V,我們都寄 FP 和 V 的 register (~100 個包裹)。hello 根本沒用 -> 全是浪費。不寄 = 快很多。**簡單。**

2. **「怎麼存」(你問的)** -- 一個包裹裝更多。現在 V 的 32 個 register,我們寄 32 次 (一次一個)。有個技巧 (LMUL) 可以一次裝 8 個 -> 32 變 4 次。**比較難。**

那個 `/dev/shm` 共享記憶體檔案,是**唯一不用排隊**的路。我們已經用它搬 V 的資料 bytes。但還是要寄 32 個包裹去告訴 CPU「現在抄 register 0... 現在 register 1...」-- 這 32 次排隊就是浪費。

content.text:
"Round-trip" = you **ask** the CPU to do one thing, then you must **wait** until it says "done." Ask + wait-for-answer-to-come-back = one round-trip.

**Why must we ask-and-wait? Why not just set the register directly?**

Because in vsim the CPU registers are **locked deep inside** the simulated hardware. You cannot touch them from outside. The only door in is the **debug unit** -- the same special door a real hardware debugger (JTAG) uses on a real chip.

That door only understands one recipe. To put a number into **one** register:

1. put the number into a mailbox slot
2. tell the door "copy the mailbox into register x5"
3. ask "done yet? done yet? done yet?" until it answers done  <- **this is the wait**

Step 3 is why it is a round-trip, not a quick one-way poke.

**Why the wait cannot be skipped:** there is only **one** mailbox. If you send the next register before this one finishes, you overwrite the work in progress. So you must wait for "done" before the next register.

**Why the wait is slow:** vsim is cycle-accurate -- it simulates the **whole chip, one clock tick at a time**. The debug unit needs ~1000 ticks to move one register. vsim must compute all ~1000 ticks of the entire chip just to let that one move finish. That ~1000-tick simulation **is** the cost of one round-trip.

So: 190 registers = 190 asks = 190 waits = ~190,000 ticks of pure waiting. That waiting is the slow part. The only way to make it faster is **fewer asks** -- which is exactly what gating (#2) and the LMUL trick do.

1. You mean that PB isn't faster than abstract command. right? 
2. why do we transfer vector registers 32 times?

content.text:
**1. Correct.** For moving **one** register, PB is not faster than an abstract command -- both pay the same single wait (~1000 ticks). The abstract command is even slightly cheaper, because it skips writing the little program first.

PB's only advantage is that **one** PB run can be written to do **many** registers at once. An abstract command is stuck at exactly one register per run.

The problem: our V sweep uses PB but still does **one register per run** -- so it pays PB's cost and gets none of PB's batching benefit. That is the waste.

**2. Because the register number is baked inside each instruction.**

`vle8.v v0, (x7)` always loads into v0. To fill v1 you need a *different* instruction, `vle8.v v1, (x7)`. The "v0" / "v1" is part of the 32-bit instruction itself -- you cannot say "load into whichever register". So 32 vector registers need 32 different instructions = 32 PB runs = 32 waits.

This is the actual loop (`program_buffer.hpp`):

```cpp
for (uint16_t i = 0; i < 32; ++i) {
    write_register_abstract(bus, regno_gpr(7), scratch_gpa + i*stride); // wait: set address
    pb = { encode_vle8_v(i, 7) };   // "vle8.v v<i>, (x7)" -- v<i> hardcoded
    exec_progbuf(bus, pb);          // wait: run the one instruction
}
```

It is actually ~2 waits per register (one to set the address pointer x7, one to run the load), so ~64 waits for the V data alone, plus the `vsetvl` setup.

**The fix (the LMUL trick):** tell the CPU to treat 8 registers as one big group (set `vtype` LMUL=8). Then a single `vle8.v v0` fills v0..v7 at once. Four instructions -- v0, v8, v16, v24 -- cover all 32. So 32 runs -> 4 runs.

content.text:
對,你的直覺是對的。讓我把重點講清楚。

**PB 跑一次 = 等一次,不管裡面放幾個 instruction。**

`exec_progbuf` 做的事:寫 instructions 進 buffer -> 下一個 "execute" 命令 -> **等一次** busy 清掉。那個 hart 會把 buffer 裡**全部**的 instruction 跑完,碰到 ebreak 停。所以:

關鍵:那 ~1000 拍是**「每次執行」的固定握手成本**(進/出 debug mode 的交握),**不是每個 instruction 的成本**。hart 跑 1 個還是 7 個 instruction,差別只有幾拍,跟 ~1000 拍比是微不足道。

所以你說的對 -- 塞 7 個 load 進去跑一次,只付**一次** ~1000 拍,不是 7 次。

**一個小修正:這個 debug module 的 PB 只能放 15 個 instruction**(共 16 格,1 格留給結束記號 ebreak),不是 32。這是硬體設計的格數。

**那為什麼現在的 code 要跑 32 次?** 因為它寫得很笨 -- 每次只放 **1 個** load,而且每個 register 的資料在不同位址,所以中間還用一個 abstract command 去改位址 x7:

```
現在 (每個 register):
  set x7 = 位址        <- 等 1 次 (abstract command)
  vle8.v v<i>, (x7)    <- 等 1 次 (PB 跑 1 個 instruction)
  = 2 次等待 × 32 = 64 次等待
```

它完全沒用到你說的批次。

**你的想法就是正解。** 把多個 load 放進同一個 buffer,位址用 buffer 裡面的 `addi` 自己加,就不用每次用 abstract command 改 x7:

```
你的想法 (一次塞 ~7 個 register):
  vle8.v v0, (x7)
  addi   x7, x7, stride
  vle8.v v1, (x7)
  addi   x7, x7, stride
  ... (2 個 instruction 一個 register, 15 格 ~= 7 個 register)
  ebreak
  = 跑一次 = 等 1 次,抓 7 個 register
  32 個 register -> 約 5 次等待 (本來 64 次)
```

**再加 LMUL=8** (一個 `vle8.v` 抓 8 個 register),那 4 個 load + 3 個 addi + ebreak = 8 格,塞得進去:

```
  vsetvl ... m8        ; 叫 CPU 把 8 個 register 當一組
  vle8.v v0,  (x7)     ; 一次抓 v0..v7
  addi   x7, x7, 8*vlenb
  vle8.v v8,  (x7)     ; v8..v15
  addi   x7, x7, 8*vlenb
  vle8.v v16, (x7)     ; v16..v23
  addi   x7, x7, 8*vlenb
  vle8.v v24, (x7)     ; v24..v31
  ebreak
  = 跑一次 = 等 1 次,抓全部 32 個 vector register
```

從 64 次等待變成大約 1 次。這就是「怎麼存」可以省的地方。

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# L11: a VLEN-1024 engine drains its full V registers -- no silent clamp.
#
# rt_c_v_fill fills v8 with 0xA5 across all vlenb bytes before the enter
# marker. The QEMU leg runs at vlen=1024 (vlenb=128, twice the old 64-byte
# wire ceiling); the plugin must drain vlenb=128 and the WHOLE register:
# the last byte of v8's slot would read 0 under the old clamp.
#
# Also pins the fast-standalone override surface: a user-supplied trailing
# `-cpu` (after `--`) replaces the built-in vlen=512, so
# `andesim run --mode fast` covers VLEN 128..1024 without a new flag.
#
# Manual TDD smoke; not auto-wired into scripts/run_e2e.sh (the fixture
# itself runs there via the normal marker/pc suite at the engine VLEN).

set -euo pipefail

SCRIPT_DIR=$(cd -- "$(dirname -- "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)
. "$SCRIPT_DIR/../lib/paths.sh"
. "$SCRIPT_DIR/../lib/log.sh"

FIXTURE="${FIXTURE:-rt_c_v_fill}"
TIMEOUT="${TIMEOUT:-120}"

hybrid_resolve_paths

SHARED_SIZE=$((128 * 1024 * 1024))
SHARED_MEM=$(mktemp -p /dev/shm vsim-vlen1024-shared.XXXXXX)
STATE_QEMU=$(mktemp)
trap 'rm -f "$SHARED_MEM" "$STATE_QEMU"' EXIT
truncate -s "$SHARED_SIZE" "$SHARED_MEM"

read_u64_le() { od -A n -j "$1" -N 8 -t u8 "$2" | tr -d ' \n'; }
read_u8()     { od -A n -j "$1" -N 1 -t u1 "$2" | tr -d ' \n'; }

V8_LAST=$((V8_FIRST + 127))         # byte 127: only present un-clamped

set +e
"$VSIM_QEMU" \
  -object "memory-backend-file,id=mem,share=on,mem-path=$SHARED_MEM,size=$SHARED_SIZE" \

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# L11: a VLEN-1024 engine drains its full V registers -- no silent clamp.
#
# rt_c_v_fill fills v8 with 0xA5 across all vlenb bytes before the enter
# marker. The QEMU leg runs at vlen=1024 (vlenb=128, twice the old 64-byte
# wire ceiling); the plugin must drain vlenb=128 and the WHOLE register:
# the last byte of v8's slot would read 0 under the old clamp.
#
# Also pins the fast-standalone override surface: a user-supplied trailing
# `-cpu` (after `--`) replaces the built-in vlen=512, so
# `andesim run --mode fast` covers VLEN 128..1024 without a new flag.
#
# Manual TDD smoke; not auto-wired into scripts/run_e2e.sh (the fixture
# itself runs there via the normal marker/pc suite at the engine VLEN).

set -euo pipefail

SCRIPT_DIR=$(cd -- "$(dirname -- "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)
. "$SCRIPT_DIR/../lib/paths.sh"
. "$SCRIPT_DIR/../lib/log.sh"

FIXTURE="${FIXTURE:-rt_c_v_fill}"
TIMEOUT="${TIMEOUT:-120}"

hybrid_resolve_paths

SHARED_SIZE=$((128 * 1024 * 1024))
SHARED_MEM=$(mktemp -p /dev/shm vsim-vlen1024-shared.XXXXXX)
STATE_QEMU=$(mktemp)
trap 'rm -f "$SHARED_MEM" "$STATE_QEMU"' EXIT
truncate -s "$SHARED_SIZE" "$SHARED_MEM"

read_u64_le() { od -A n -j "$1" -N 8 -t u8 "$2" | tr -d ' \n'; }
read_u8()     { od -A n -j "$1" -N 1 -t u1 "$2" | tr -d ' \n'; }

V8_FIRST=$((1320 + 8 * 128))        # vreg[8 * HYBRID_VLEN_BYTES_MAX]
V8_LAST=$((V8_FIRST + 127))         # byte 127: only present un-clamped

"$VSIM_QEMU" \
  -object "memory-backend-file,id=mem,share=on,mem-path=$SHARED_MEM,size=$SHARED_SIZE" \

QEMU1_RC=$?

[ "$QEMU1_RC" -eq 200 ] || fail "QEMU 1 expected exit 200 on marker drain, got $QEMU1_RC"

ok "QEMU 1 drained vlenb=128 (VLEN 1024)"

B_LAST=$(read_u8 "$V8_LAST" "$STATE_QEMU")

## What changed (vsim repo, 4 files, +168/-15)

`src/hybrid/program_buffer.hpp` -- `pb_v_data_sweep` now packs `(vle8.v/vse8.v ; addi)` pairs into each Program-Buffer execution and advances the base pointer `x7` with the in-buffer `addi`, instead of one execution + one `x7` abstract write per register. Added `encode_addi`.

## TDD trail
- **RED** `encode_addi` golden test -> compile error -> **GREEN** (golden `addi x7,x7,128 = 0x08038393`, confirmed against `riscv64-elf-as`).
- **RED** batching test (`exec count == 6`, `x7 staged once`, `addi present`) failed against the old sweep (33 execs, 32 `x7` writes, no addi) -> **GREEN** after the rewrite.
- Updated the two existing sweep tests (`resume_driver`, `state_drain`) that asserted the old per-register `x7` staging.

## Verification
- **All hybrid unit tests green** (program_buffer 16, resume_driver 38, state_drain 25, +11 others). The lone `state_abi` failure is pre-existing v3/v4 submodule skew in files I never touched.
- **3 V fixtures pass `--verify`** (rebuilt `sim_ax45mpv_premium`): `rt_c_v_regs`, `rt_c_v_csrs`, `rt_c_v_matmul`. `state-diff` reports **byte-identical** V state vs the QEMU oracle (146 fields). This is the real proof -- a wrong `addi` stride, `x7`-persistence bug, or off-by-one would surface as a V mismatch.
- `rt_c_v_fill` fails at the **QEMU leg** (step 1, before vsim runs) -- it is the dedicated vlen=1024 fixture; pre-existing and orthogonal to this vsim-side change.

## The win (per direction, for the V data sweep)
| | exec commands | x7 abstract writes |
|---|---|---|
| before | 33 | 32 |
| after | **6** | **1** |

~67 round-trips -> ~9 per direction; a V handoff (resume + drain) drops ~116 round-trips, each ~1000 sim cycles in the busy-poll.

- **Not committed** -- per your workflow I commit only when you ask.
- **LMUL=8 grouping** is the further step (one `vle8.v` loads 8 registers -> 32 loads collapse toward a single execution), but it needs the scratch repacked to `vlenb` stride. Want me to commit this first, then layer LMUL?

You are improving the quality of the changed code, not hunting for bugs. Review
it for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude issues, then fix what you
find. Do not look for correctness bugs — that is what `/code-review` is for.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Review (4 cleanup agents in parallel)

Launch **4 independent review agents** via the Agent tool, all in a
single message so they run concurrently. Pass each agent the diff and one of
the four angles below. Each returns its findings with `file`, `line`, a
one-line `summary`, and the concrete cost (what is duplicated, wasted, or
harder to maintain).

### Reuse

Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change is implemented at the right depth, not as a fragile
bandaid. Special cases layered on shared infrastructure are a sign the fix
isn't deep enough — prefer generalizing the underlying mechanism over adding
special cases.

## Phase 2 — Apply the fixes

Wait for all four agents to complete, dedup findings that point at the same
line or mechanism, and fix each remaining one directly. Skip any finding whose
fix would change intended behavior, require changes well outside the reviewed
diff, or that you judge to be a false positive — note the skip rather than
arguing with it. Finish with a brief summary of what was fixed and what was
skipped (or confirm the code was already clean).

input.content:
perf(hybrid): batch the V-data sweep into fewer Program-Buffer executions

The V-register sweep issued one Program-Buffer execution per register plus one
abstract x7 write per register -- 33 PB executions + 32 x7 writes each
direction. Each is a halted-hart Debug-Module round-trip (~1000 sim cycles
spent in the busy-poll), so the cost is the NUMBER of executions, not the bytes
moved (the data itself rides the shared mmap).

Pack (vle8.v/vse8.v ; addi) pairs into each execution and advance the base
pointer x7 with the in-buffer addi, so x7 is staged ONCE and 32 registers cost
ceil(32/7)=5 executions: 33 -> 6 PB executions and 32 -> 1 x7 write per
direction (~67 -> ~9 DM round-trips). x7 persists across executions (the hart
stays halted), so each batch resumes advancing where the last stopped. Adds
encode_addi.

The drained V state is byte-identical: verified by --verify (state-diff) on
rt_c_v_regs, rt_c_v_csrs, and rt_c_v_matmul against the QEMU oracle.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

`/simplify → 4 cleanup agents in parallel → apply the fixes`

You are improving the quality of the changed code, not hunting for bugs. Review
it for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude issues, then fix what you
find. Do not look for correctness bugs — that is what `/code-review` is for.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Review (4 cleanup agents in parallel)

Launch **4 independent review agents** via the Agent tool, all in a
single message so they run concurrently. Pass each agent the diff and one of
the four angles below. Each returns its findings with `file`, `line`, a
one-line `summary`, and the concrete cost (what is duplicated, wasted, or
harder to maintain).

### Reuse

Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change is implemented at the right depth, not as a fragile
bandaid. Special cases layered on shared infrastructure are a sign the fix
isn't deep enough — prefer generalizing the underlying mechanism over adding
special cases.

## Phase 2 — Apply the fixes

Wait for all four agents to complete, dedup findings that point at the same
line or mechanism, and fix each remaining one directly. Skip any finding whose
fix would change intended behavior, require changes well outside the reviewed
diff, or that you judge to be a false positive — note the skip rather than
arguing with it. Finish with a brief summary of what was fixed and what was
skipped (or confirm the code was already clean).

~8.5s -- matching the batching commit, exactly as you observed. You're right, and here's the precise reason.

## Why LMUL doesn't move hello

hello transports **FP + V + ANDES + M_EXT by capability** (flags=0x1f), though it uses none of them. Its inject is ~130 DMI round-trips, roughly:

| block | round-trips | LMUL touches it? |
|---|---|---|
| FPR f0-f31 + fcsr | ~33 | no |
| Andes CSRs | ~13-20 | no |
| M-ext CSRs | ~17 | no |
| GPR x1-x31 | 31 | no |
| M-mode CSRs | ~12 | no |
| **V-data sweep** | **~5** | **yes** |
| V scalar CSRs | ~8 | no |

The **V-data sweep is ~5 of ~130**. The *batching* commit already cut it from ~66 to ~9; LMUL takes ~9 to ~5 -- about 4 round-trips, which is inside wall-clock noise. LMUL only ever optimizes the V-sweep slice, and that slice is small relative to the abstract-command blocks that dominate. So it's marginal not just for hello but broadly (even matmul's sweep is small next to its ROI + other blocks).

## The real lever for hello is #2 (usage gating), not the sweep

hello's `mstatus.FS=Initial` (no FP used) and `vtype.vill=1` (no V configured). Gating transport on *usage* skips **FP (~33) + V (~13) = ~46 round-trips (~35% of inject)** -- a real cut. The sweep mechanism was never hello's bottleneck; transporting blocks hello never touched is.

## /simplify results (the review finished)

- **Altitude flagged a "CRITICAL: kVtypeE8M8=0xC3 is LMUL=1, should be 0xD8" -- that is a FALSE POSITIVE.** `0xC3` = vma|vta | vsew=000 (e8) | vlmul=**011 (m8)`; the agent transposed the vsew[5:3] and vlmul[2:0] fields (0xD8 would actually be e64/m1). And the proof is empirical: `--verify` passed on all 3 V fixtures with all 32 V registers byte-identical -- if vtype were m1, only v0/v8/v16/v24 would load and the other 28 would be garbage. Grouping works.
- Real findings are minor: make `read_v_from_scratch` zero its own padding (robustness), and a cross-file comment tying "stager packs at vlenb" to "sweep reads at vlenb". Low value.

## Recommendation

LMUL is **uncommitted** and marginal-for-real-complexity (packed scratch + signature change) for a ~4-round-trip gain. I'd **revert it** (keep the committed batching, which captured the actual V-sweep win) and **implement #2** -- the ~46-round-trip win for scalar programs like hello.

content.text:
Committed LMUL: **`1838445`** (8 files; `external/systemc-cci` + `build_vsim.sh` untouched).

Now your question -- **yes, and this is the biggest remaining lever, far bigger than the V work.** It targets exactly the blocks that dominate hello (GPR 31 + FPR 33 + CSRs ~48), which LMUL never touched.

## Why it works (same reason V does)

The cost is the **busy-poll count**, not bytes. An abstract GPR write costs one ~1000-cycle poll; a PB execution also costs one poll but runs up to 15 instructions. So marshalling values through the mmap (free) and loading them with a PB sweep collapses many polls into a few.

**GPR:** stage 31 values (248 B) in a scratch block, then `ld x1,0(base); ld x2,8(base); ...` -- `ld`'s 12-bit offset (±2048) spans all 31 slots, so no `addi` needed. 31 loads / 15 slots = ~3 PB executions + 1 abstract write to seed the base. **31 -> ~4 round-trips.**

**FPR:** identical with `fld` (FP already enabled via `mstatus.FS`). **33 -> ~4.**

**CSRs** (Andes/M-ext/M-mode, the other big chunk): can't `ld` a CSR, so `ld xN,off(base); csrw <csr>,xN` -- 2 insns each, ~7 CSRs per execution. **~48 -> ~10.**

Estimated inject: **~130 -> ~30 round-trips (~4x)**. GPR+FPR alone is ~56 fewer -- that's what actually cuts hello's ~8.5s.

## Honest complications
- **Base-register ordering**: the base GPR is itself architectural -- seed it with the scratch GPA, load the other 30 first, load the base's own value **last** (the V sweep already uses/restores x5/x6/x7 this way, so it composes).
- **Scratch layout**: add GPR/FPR/CSR sub-regions alongside the V page (all ride the mmap).
- **Blast radius**: this rewrites the *core* restore path in `ResumeDriver` (and `StateDrain` for `--verify`), bigger than the V sweep. Must be proven with `--verify`.
- **Drain side** benefits only `--verify` runs (the minimal-drain #1 already skips drain otherwise).

## One alternative worth a quick check first
The RISC-V Debug Module has optional **`abstractauto` + `aarpostincrement`**: stream a contiguous regno range (x1..x31, f0..f31) with one command setup and no per-register poll -- **no scratch, no base register**, simpler than the PB sweep. It only works if the vsim DM implements those bits (CSRs are non-contiguous, so they'd still need the PB `ld+csrw` path). If supported, it's the cleaner win for GPR/FPR.

**Suggested path:** prototype GPR first (smallest, proves the pattern and *measures* the real poll-latency gain), then FPR, then CSRs. Want me to check the DM's `abstractauto` support and prototype GPR?

content.text:
Two decisive findings:
1. **Access Register runs a generated ~5-instruction program on the hart** (`_abs_reg_access_prog0..4`), so each abstract command's cost is real *execution*, not just transport -- meaning fewer **executions** is what wins (the PB block-load), not abstractauto.
2. **No register post-increment** (only `aampostincr` for *memory*). Without `aarpostincrement`, abstractauto would re-write the *same* regno every time -- useless for streaming x1..x31. **So the abstractauto path is out; PB block-load is the way**, exactly as you framed it.

Found it: `ae350_config.vh:29: PLATFORM_PLDM_PROGBUF_SIZE = 8`. The real Program Buffer is **8 slots**, not the 16 that `kProgbufMaxInsns=15` assumes. content.text:
**Root cause found.** The probe proves x1 and x30 load correctly but x31 = 0 right after the sweep. x31's slot is the mmap's **final 8 bytes** (0x8000ff8); x30 (0x8000ff0) works. The guest RTL doesn't return the very last word of the shared mapping — V never hit this because V data sits in the bottom half of the scratch page.

Done — GPR block-load prototype works: **all 8 fixtures PASS `--verify`**, hello ~7.77s (from ~8.5s). Probe fully removed. Now your two questions.

## What was wrong with x31

The block-load stages all 31 GPR values into a scratch area at the **very top** of the shared memory mapping, then runs `ld x1,0(x31); ld x2,8(x31); ...` in the Program Buffer, using **x31 as the base pointer**. x31 was loaded last, from its own slot — and that slot was the **final 8 bytes of the whole mapping**.

The guest (vsim RTL) does **not** return that final word. The host wrote `0xa0..1f` there, but the guest `ld` from that address read **0**. So x31 came back 0. Every other register (x1..x30) sat just below that final word and loaded fine.

A probe (read x1/x30/x31 back right after the sweep) proved it:
```
gpr_gpa=0x8000f08   x1=0xa0..01  x30=0xa0..1e  x31=0x0
```
x30 at `0x8000ff0` = correct; x31 at `0x8000ff8` (the mapping's last word) = 0.

**Why the V tests never caught it:** V data only fills the **bottom** half of the scratch page (2048 bytes at vlenb=64). It never touches the top word. So V passed while x31 — at the very top — failed. Two earlier bugs hid behind each other: first I assumed a 16-slot Program Buffer (it is really 8, from the RTL `PLATFORM_PLDM_PROGBUF_SIZE=8`), which made x9+ fail; fixing that left only x31.

## How I resolved it

Don't put anything the guest must read in that final word:

1. **Block-load only x1..x30** via the `ld`-sweep — they all sit below the final word (the probe already showed them correct).
2. **Restore x31 with one direct abstract write** of its value, not from a scratch slot. x31 is the base pointer anyway, so it is never overwritten by an `ld` and stays valid through the whole sweep.
3. Its would-be slot (the final word) is left as an **unused guard**.

Cost is still a big win: **2 abstract writes + ~5 PB executions** for 31 registers, versus 31 abstract writes before — hello dropped ~1s.

Honest caveat: I localized the failure empirically to the mapping's final word; I did not fully trace *why* the RTL drops it. The guard is a correct, documented workaround for this prototype. The clean production fix is a **dedicated GPR scratch page** (map a second extra page instead of sharing the top of the V page) — then no guard is needed and the layout is not coupled to V. Uncommitted (7 files, +206); say the word and I commit, or I can do the dedicated-page version first.

skills.content:
`/simplify → 4 cleanup agents in parallel → apply the fixes`

You are improving the quality of the changed code, not hunting for bugs. Review
it for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude issues, then fix what you
find. Do not look for correctness bugs — that is what `/code-review` is for.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Review (4 cleanup agents in parallel)

Launch **4 independent review agents** via the Agent tool, all in a
single message so they run concurrently. Pass each agent the diff and one of
the four angles below. Each returns its findings with `file`, `line`, a
one-line `summary`, and the concrete cost (what is duplicated, wasted, or
harder to maintain).

### Reuse

Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change is implemented at the right depth, not as a fragile
bandaid. Special cases layered on shared infrastructure are a sign the fix
isn't deep enough — prefer generalizing the underlying mechanism over adding
special cases.

## Phase 2 — Apply the fixes

Wait for all four agents to complete, dedup findings that point at the same
line or mechanism, and fix each remaining one directly. Skip any finding whose
fix would change intended behavior, require changes well outside the reviewed
diff, or that you judge to be a false positive — note the skip rather than
arguing with it. Finish with a brief summary of what was fixed and what was
skipped (or confirm the code was already clean).

lastPrompt: find the root cause why RTL drops that address

content.text:
Root cause found. It is a real off-by-one in the vsim memory model's bounds check -- the last word of RAM is unreachable by the guest. It is the SystemC TLM target model (`SimpleMemory`), not the Verilator RTL core.

## The bug

`src/platform/simple_memory.hpp:84`:
```cpp
if (region.contains({addr, addr + len})) [[likely]] {
```

`{addr, addr + len}` builds a temporary `MemoryRegion`. But that constructor treats its 2nd argument as an **inclusive** end and stores `end_address = arg + 1` (`memory_region.hpp:29`). The access's `addr + len` is already the **exclusive** end. So the temporary becomes `[addr, addr + len + 1)` -- **one byte too long**.

Then `contains()` checks `other.end_address <= this->end_address`, i.e. it requires `addr + len + 1 <= region.end_address`. That reserves one extra byte past every access. Any access whose exclusive end lands exactly on `region.end_address` -- the final byte of RAM -- is falsely rejected as out-of-bounds (`TLM_ADDRESS_ERROR`), so the guest `ld` never receives the staged value and x31 stays at its reset 0.

## Proof (probe numbers: base=0, mmap=0x8001000)

`region = [0, 0x8001000)`. Constructed as `{base, base+size-1}` then `+1` -> `end_address = 0x8001000`.

| reg | addr | temp.end_address (addr+len+1) | `<= 0x8001000`? |
|-----|------|-------------------------------|-----------------|
| x30 | 0x8000ff0 | 0x8000ff9 | yes -> loads |
| x31 | 0x8000ff8 | 0x8001001 | **no -> rejected** |

x31's slot is the mmap's last word. x1..x30 sit below it, so only x31 fails.

## Why it hid until now

It only bites the **final byte** of a region. Normal programs never park data at the exact top of RAM, and the V-data sweep lives at the **bottom** of the scratch page. The GPR-block-load scheme is the first code to touch the last word, so it exposed a latent bug that was always there (it also makes the last word of the 2.25 GB default RAM region unreachable -- just never hit).

The host writes 0xa0..1f straight into the mmap (bypasses this check), so `/dev/shm` shows the value; only the guest read path hits the bounds check. That is exactly the host-sees / guest-reads-0 asymmetry we saw.

## The proper fix

The temporary abuses the inclusive-end constructor. Replace the foot-gun with a half-open access check on `MemoryRegion`:
```cpp
auto contains_access(addr_type addr, addr_type len) const noexcept -> bool
{ return addr >= base_address && addr < end_address && len <= end_address - addr; }
```
Use it at both `simple_memory.hpp:84,86`. This is **strictly more permissive** than today: it admits exactly the previously-rejected final-byte accesses and rejects nothing that already worked, so no fixture can regress. Once the last word is reachable, the guard is unnecessary -- block-load all 31 GPRs and drop the separate x31 abstract write.

input.detail:
Root cause: simple_memory.hpp:84,86 call region.contains({addr, addr+len}); the MemoryRegion ctor treats arg2 as inclusive and stores end+1, so the temp is [addr, addr+len+1) -- one byte too long. contains() then rejects any access whose exclusive end == region.end_address (the final RAM word). Fix via TDD + Tidy-First, 2 commits in /home/nick/work/vsim_andesim:

Commit 1 (behavioral, decoder fix):
- RED: test MemoryRegion::contains_access(addr,len) last-word case in src/tests/platform/memory_region.test.cpp.
- GREEN: add contains_access(addr,len) { addr>=base && addr<end && len<=end-addr } to memory_region.hpp; use at simple_memory.hpp:84,86. Strictly more permissive -> no regression.
- Run platform + hybrid unit tests.

Commit 2 (behavioral, remove guard):
- v_regfile_xfer.hpp stage_gpr_to_scratch: loop i<32 (stage x1..x31), update comment.
- resume_driver.hpp restore_gprs_via_pb: loop k<32 (block-load x1..x31), drop separate x31 abstract write + gpr31_value param; update resume() call site.
- Update v_regfile_xfer.test.cpp + resume_driver.test.cpp.
- Rebuild sim, --verify fixtures (rt_all_gprs, rt_c_hello, rt_c_v_regs, rt_csr_survival, ...).

function(vsim_add_test TARGET SOURCE)
  add_executable(${TARGET} EXCLUDE_FROM_ALL ${SOURCE})
  target_include_directories(${TARGET} SYSTEM PRIVATE ${VSIM_INCLUDE_DIRS})
  target_include_directories(${TARGET} PRIVATE
    "${CMAKE_BINARY_DIR}"
    "${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/src"
    "${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/src/utils")
  target_include_directories(${TARGET} SYSTEM PRIVATE
    "${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/external/doctest/doctest")
  target_compile_options(${TARGET} PRIVATE ${VSIM_COMPILE_FLAGS})
  target_compile_definitions(${TARGET} PRIVATE ${VSIM_COMPILE_DEFS})
  target_link_options(${TARGET} PRIVATE ${VSIM_LINK_FLAGS})
  add_test(NAME ${TARGET} COMMAND $<TARGET_FILE:${TARGET}>)
